why: Every team versions its code, SQL and pipelines with Git. A clean GitHub profile is also the first thing recruiters open.
outcome: create a repository, commit cleanly, work on branches, open a pull request and fix a simple conflict.

lessons.title: Commits: the history of your project
text: Git takes snapshots of your files. You choose what goes into the next snapshot (staging with git add), then record it with a message (git commit).
A good commit does one thing and its message says why, in the present tense: 'Add salary filter to search'.
points: git status tells you what changed and what is staged.
git diff shows unstaged changes; git diff --staged shows what will be committed.
git log --oneline gives a compact history.
Use a .gitignore for secrets, data dumps and generated files.

example.code:
git init
git add README.md src/
git commit -m "Add first version of the job scraper"
git log --oneline

lessons.title: Branches and pull requests
text: A branch is a movable pointer to a line of work. Create one per feature or fix so main always stays working.
On GitHub, push the branch and open a pull request (PR): teammates review the diff, CI runs tests, then you merge.
points: git switch -c feature/salary-filter creates and moves to a branch.
git push -u origin feature/salary-filter publishes it.
Keep PRs small: they get reviewed faster and break less.
Describe what changed, why, and how you tested it in the PR description.

example.code:
git switch -c feature/salary-filter
# ... edit files ...
git add -A
git commit -m "Filter offers by minimum salary"
git push -u origin feature/salary-filter
# then open a Pull Request on GitHub

lessons.title: Stay in sync and fix conflicts
text: Others change main while you work. git pull brings their commits into your branch; if you both edited the same lines, Git asks you to resolve a conflict.
A conflict is just text with markers. Keep the right version, delete the markers, add and commit.
points: git fetch downloads changes without touching your files; git pull = fetch + merge.
git restore file throws away local changes to a file (careful).
git revert <commit> undoes a commit safely by adding a new one.

example.code:
git switch feature/salary-filter
git pull origin main      # conflict in search.py
# edit search.py, keep the right lines, remove <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>>
git add search.py
git commit                # completes the merge

lessons.title: Undo safely: restore, revert, reset and stash
text: Everyone commits the wrong thing sometimes. What matters is choosing an undo that does not hurt your teammates. On your own unpushed work you can rewrite freely; on a shared branch you add a new commit that undoes the old one instead of rewriting history.

git revert creates that undo commit. git reset moves your branch back and is for local history only. git stash puts unfinished work aside so you can switch branches, and git reflog remembers where your branch pointed, so almost nothing is ever truly lost.
points: Pushed already? Use revert, not reset.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged.
git reset --hard throws away uncommitted work: check git status first.
Interactive rebase (git rebase -i) cleans up your own commits before opening a pull request.

example.code:
git restore app.py              # drop local changes to a file
git restore --staged app.py     # unstage, keep the changes
git commit --amend              # fix the last commit (not pushed yet)
git stash push -m "wip"         # put work aside
git stash pop                   # bring it back
git revert 3f2c9ab              # new commit that undoes 3f2c9ab (safe on shared branches)
git reflog                      # find a 'lost' commit
example.note: revert is the safe default on main; reset and amend are for work nobody else has pulled.

items: Create and switch to a branch
Merge a branch into the current one
Discard local edits to a file
Undo a commit with a new commit

pitfalls: Committing passwords or API keys. Even after deletion they stay in history: rotate the key.
Working directly on main and pushing broken code.
Huge commits mixing unrelated changes with messages like 'update'.
Using git push --force on a shared branch.

exercises.q: You committed to main by mistake but have not pushed. How do you move that commit to a new branch?
exercises.answer:
git branch my-feature        # new branch points at your commit
git reset --hard HEAD~1      # move main back one commit
git switch my-feature

exercises.q: How do you see which commit changed a given line of a file?
exercises.answer: git blame <file> shows, for each line, the last commit and author that changed it. On GitHub, the 'Blame' button does the same.

exercises.q: Write a .gitignore for a Python data project.
A commit a1b2c3d pushed to main an hour ago broke the build. Others have pulled since. Undo it safely.

interview.a: Both integrate changes from one branch into another. merge keeps history as it happened and adds a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of the other branch for a linear history. Never rebase commits others already use.

interview.q: How do you undo a commit that is already pushed?
interview.a: Use git revert <sha>: it creates a new commit that reverses the change, without rewriting shared history.

interview.q: What makes a good pull request?
interview.a: Small and focused, a clear title, a description of what and why, how it was tested, screenshots for UI, and passing CI.

interview.q: What is the difference between git revert and git reset?
interview.a: revert adds a new commit that undoes the changes of an earlier one, so history is preserved and it is safe on shared branches. reset moves the branch pointer back, removing commits from the branch history; it is fine for local, unpushed work but rewriting pushed history forces others to fix their copies, so I avoid it on shared branches.
